To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the neural responses elicited by unrecognizable texform stimuli were sufficient to elicate the large-scale organizations along the entire ventoral pathway, and that the structure in the patterns elicited by the texforms was well-predicted by curvature features and the representations of intermediate layers of a CNN.
the large-scale organization in human object-selective cortex can be explained by a class of unrecognizable texform stimuli that preserve some mid-level features of objects.

a class of unrecognizable stimuli (texforms), despite being visually unrecognizable, elicit large-scale neural patterns that are well predicted by curvature information and by mid-level representations from a deep convolutional network, suggesting that a large portion of ventral pathway organization can be explained without the need for object recognition.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the large-scale organization and functional properties of human visual cortex.
how the human brain processes visual information.
the question of how the brain represents and processes visual information.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the large-scale organization is not explained by high-level object recognition but by low- or mid-level perceptual information.
the large-scale organization is driven by the mid-level features of animacy, object size, and curvature.
the ventral stream is organized by mid-level features that are not necessarily object recognition related.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a substantial portion (but not all) of the organization in the human ventral pathway is explained by mid-level features, without requiring explicit object recognition.
the ventral visual cortex organizes its responses into a hierarchy of increasingly abstract representations of objects and scenes.
a substantial portion, if not most, of the ventral organization is driven by primitive mid-level features that distinguish animals and objects from each other and big objects from smaller objects.
The main takeaway from our work is that
much of ventural stream organization can be understood by relatively primitive midlevel features without requiring explicit object recognition.
much of ventural stream organization can be predicted by relatively simple mid-level features.
much of the organization of object-selective ventral stream cortex can be explained by mid-level visual features without requiring explicit object recognition.
